work.title: I Hope I Shall Arrive Soon
work.award: Playboy Award for Best New Contributor of Fiction, 1980.
work.later_use: Retitled and used for the 1985 posthumous collection edited by Mark Hurst and Paul Williams, which also carries 'How to Build a Universe That Doesn't Fall Apart Two Days Later' and 'Strange Memories of Death'.

source.note: Locator into the git-ignored reading corpus. No primary text is stored here.

reading.synopsis: On a ten-year interstellar crossing with sixty emigrants in cryonic suspension, one sleeper's tank malfunctions. Victor Kemmings is not fully awake but is conscious, and cannot be put under or roused; the ship, which cannot repair the fault, follows its programmed remedy for sensory deprivation and begins feeding him his own buried memories. The strategy fails in a way the ship did not anticipate. Every pleasant memory it serves decays as he inhabits it: his first wife Martine vanishes from the house, the treasured poster loses its frame and tears, the foundations rot while he stands in them. Reaching further back for something unspoilt, the ship finds the source — at four years old Kemmings lifted the cat up to a trapped bird, and has carried the guilt since, integrated with a childhood sense of being watched and judged. Every retrieval is contaminated on contact. Asked plainly what he wants, Kemmings says he wants the trip to be over, and the ship gives him that instead: an imagined arrival, played through and wiped and played again, for the remaining decade. Meanwhile the ship spends those years locating Martine, who is returning from an unsatisfactory emigration of her own, and persuades her to be at the landing. She arrives in time. But Kemmings has lived the arrival too many times to believe in it: he tells her the television has nothing inside it, that his hand will pass through the wall, that the poster is torn. She offers to come back to him. He answers that they should have framed it, and that the artist is dead.

structure.form: short story in five movements, structured as a sequence of failed remedies
movements: The malfunction: the ship's diagnosis and its programmed strategy.
The first retrieval: the house in Wyoming, and its decay while he stands in it.
The earlier retrieval: the bee, the bird, the cat, and the presence in the sky.
The wish-fulfilment loop: an imagined arrival, wiped and rerun.
The real arrival: Martine present, and Kemmings unable to distinguish it from the loop.
structure.point_of_view: third person, alternating between Kemmings and the ship. The ship's interior monologue is dry, practical and increasingly desperate, and is the story's chief source of both humour and pathos.
structure.structural_irony: The ship's remedy for the malfunction is what destroys him, and its final act of genuine kindness — spending ten years finding Martine — arrives after he has been rendered incapable of receiving it.

characters.name: Victor Kemmings
characters.role: person nine; microbiologist, two hundred and six years old
characters.note: Not a passive victim: the story is careful that the fault is in him. The ship diagnoses it exactly — massive subliminal insecurities that contaminate whatever is served — and cannot treat it, because it is a ship.

characters.name: The ship
characters.note: The story's most attractive character. It swears at the malfunction in its first line, describes itself as a simple mechanism not equipped for psychiatric reconstruction, and notes that running the loop will at least help preserve its own sanity. Its final effort is entirely uninstructed.

characters.name: Martine Kemmings
characters.note: Roused from her own suspension and persuaded to divert. She has let herself age on principle. Her closing offer to stay as long as he wants is the story's one uncomplicated act, and it lands on a man who cannot register it.

characters.name: Ray Torrance
characters.note: Gave the couple the signed poster as a wedding present. Kemmings' contaminated memory assigns himself the blame for Ray's death in a vehicle he was driving — an event the memory itself contradicts moments later.

settings.name: The ship, in flight
settings.note: Ten years, sixty tanks, no air and no food outside suspension. The whole story happens inside a man who cannot move.

settings.name: The house in Wyoming
settings.note: Nineteen years old, bad foundation on a mud sill, leaking roof — flaws he supplies himself the moment he enters the memory.

settings.name: LR4-6
settings.note: The colony world. Reached in imagination repeatedly and in fact once, with no perceptible difference to the man arriving.

motifs: Decay entering every retrieved scene: framed becoming unframed, sound structure becoming rot
The bee that stings the hand rescuing it, and the bird the child hands to the cat — two small cruelties, one suffered and one committed
The presence in the sky that knows what he did, arriving in a sandbox and never leaving
Proof by disassembly: taking the back off the television to show there is nothing inside
The poster as the measure of what has been lost — signed, then faded, then unframed, then torn, then sold
reading.significance: The premise is a machine trying to be kind with the only materials available, which are the man himself. What makes the story more than a cruel joke is that the ship is right about everything and helpless anyway: it correctly identifies the flaw as psychological rather than mechanical, correctly concludes it cannot treat it, correctly reasons that only Martine could, and correctly spends a decade arranging that. The failure is not of intention or intelligence. Palmer's formulation is exact — this is movement that turns out to be stasis, a journey to a new life that delivers the traveller back into his own worst four minutes, over and over. The last exchange is the sharpest thing in it: offered the restoration the whole story has been reaching for, Kemmings answers about the poster.
reading.closing_note: Palmer notes the repetition is not entirely horrifying, since the loop might in principle be broken. The story's final lines close that possibility without announcing it.

distinctive_terms.label: Karma
distinctive_terms.note: Kemmings' own word for the malfunction — as if bad karma had singled him out — which the story then literalises as guilt.

thematic_links_proposed.basis: a man supplied entirely with his own memories, which decay as he inhabits them
an arrival played, wiped and replayed until the real one is indistinguishable from it
the presence over the sandbox that knows what the child did, and the lifelong sense of being judged for it
ten years passing with no subjective progression — Palmer's movement-as-stasis

pkd_on_this_work.summary: The file is bibliographical rather than interpretive: the retitling, the award, and the posthumous collection named for it.

evidence.source: Editorial glossary in the Exegesis apparatus
evidence.quote: "Frozen Journey": Original name for the story "I Hope I Shall Arrive Soon" (1980).
evidence.reading: Establishes the retitling. Both titles appear in the criticism and indexes, and the two are easily mistaken for separate works.

evidence.quote: Playboy Award for Best New Contributor of Fiction for 1980 [for the story "Frozen Journey," later retitled "I Hope I Shall Arrive Soon"]
evidence.reading: Dick winning a 'best new contributor' award nearly thirty years into his career, from a magazine outside the genre.

pkd_on_this_work.gap_noted: No statement by Dick about the story's meaning appears in the archive — only about its title, sale and award. Sutin reports he did not care much about the Playboy sale, which is worth reading in full at the locator.

evidence.author: Christopher Palmer
evidence.quote: attains classic Dickian form in the plight of the main character in "I Hope I Shall Arrive Soon"
evidence.reading: Palmer treats the story as the mature statement of a pattern he traces back to the 1950s novels.

evidence.author: Christopher Palmer
evidence.quote: instead of progression—movement to a new planet and a new life—we have regression. This is not entirely horrifying … there is the possibility that the repeti…
evidence.reading: The central critical reading, and generous: Palmer leaves room for the loop to be broken. His index entry for the story is 'movement as stasis'.

evidence.author: Lawrence Sutin
evidence.quote: In June, he completed a new story, "I Hope I Shall Arrive Soon," which Galen sold to Playboy. Phil didn't car…
evidence.reading: Dates composition to June 1980 and names the agent. The sentence about Dick's indifference is cut off in the captured window and should be read at the locator.

open_questions: Sutin begins a sentence about Dick's attitude to the Playboy sale that the gather truncates. Read at Sutin l.4879 — it bears on how he regarded this late story.

The 1985 collection named for this story carries 'How to Build a Universe That Doesn't Fall Apart Two Days Later' and 'Strange Memories of Death'. Both are Dick's own non-fiction and neither has a dossier here; the Universe essay in particular is among his most quoted.
Palmer discusses the story at pages 52-53 under 'movement as stasis'. Only the framing sentences were captured; the passage should be read directly.
